notes.b: Leisure is time, not an activity. An activity counts as leisure when the person chooses it freely in time left over after necessary tasks.
points: Leisure is the residual time (the time left over) after essential activities have been completed.
Essential activities include paid work, travel to work, school and study, sleep, meals, personal care, household tasks and caring for dependants. These come first, so they are not leisure.
The individual chooses how to spend leisure time, for ease, relaxation or enjoyment. Because it is freely chosen, leisure is not the same as free time spent on chores.
Leisure pursuits are the activities a person chooses within leisure time, such as sport, music, reading, hobbies, crafts, gardening, socialising, drama, games, cinema and travel.
The same activity can be work for one person and leisure for another, for example gardening or cooking, depending on whether it is chosen and enjoyed.
Leisure can be active (sport, walking, dance) or passive (reading, TV, listening to music), and can be done alone, with friends or with family.
Sport is only one form of leisure, so do not treat leisure and sport as the same thing.
notes.tip: When asked to define leisure, say it is the time left after essential activities, chosen freely, for ease, relaxation and enjoyment. Define it as time, not as an activity and not as doing nothing.

notes.h: Function and value of leisure in today's society
notes.b: Leisure does more than fill spare time. It gives individuals, families and society a set of benefits, which matter more today because many jobs are sedentary and pressured.
points: Relaxation: leisure relieves the stress and fatigue that come from paid work, study and daily demands, so people recover and cope better.
Physical wellbeing: active leisure improves fitness, weight control, heart health and strong bones and muscles, and helps prevent illness. This matters more as many jobs involve sitting.
Skill development: leisure allows people to learn and practise new skills, from swimming to a musical instrument.
Challenge: competitive and creative pursuits give a sense of achievement and personal growth.
Social interaction: leisure brings people together, forming friendships and wider social networks and community involvement, which reduces isolation.
Family bonding: shared leisure builds relationships, communication and shared memories between family members.
Modelling: parents who use free time constructively are role models, showing children how to do the same.
Work-life balance: leisure offsets the demands of work and helps people sustain their working lives, staying productive and avoiding burnout. It also gives enjoyment and gratifies the senses.
notes.tip: For a discuss question, give a developed point for each of several functions: relaxation, physical wellbeing, skills, challenge, social interaction, family bonding, role modelling and work-life balance.

notes.b: Leisure benefits the wider community as well as individuals, because what people do in their free time adds up across a whole society.
points: A healthier population results when many people take part in active leisure, which reduces demands on health services.
Tourism and sport industries grow from people's demand for leisure activities and travel, which provides jobs and activity in the economy.
Community spirit is strengthened when people join clubs, teams and local events together.

notes.b: Leisure can be pursued by a person on their own or shared by a household. Each kind gives different benefits, and families need to balance both.
points: Individual leisure: a person chooses and pursues an activity alone or with a group that is not their family, such as a solo hobby, running or a club.
Family leisure: members of one household take part together, such as family outings, walks, cycling, picnics, meals out, board games, cooking, holidays, sport or games at home.
Family leisure builds bonds, communication and a shared identity, and gives children common experiences and memories.
Family leisure needs activities suitable for all ages and a cost the family can manage, so everyone can take part.
Individual leisure allows a person to develop personal interests, independence and identity, which can benefit the whole family.

notes.h: Physical and social development through leisure
notes.b: Leisure helps people develop in different ways. Physical and social development are two of the areas examiners name, so give each its own heading in an answer.
points: Physical development: sports and active pursuits build muscle tone, improve fitness and increase energy levels.
Physical development: coordination is developed through activities such as ball games, dance and gymnastics, and skills such as swimming are learned.

Physical development: weight-bearing activities, such as walking, running and dancing, help reduce the risk of osteoporosis (a condition where bones become weak and brittle) and help with weight control.
Social development: team sports require co-operation, communication and sharing of responsibility.
Social development: winning and losing teach people to cope with success and failure, which they meet in wider life.
Social development: joining a club or team helps a person make new friends, expand their social circle and feel they belong to a community.
Social development: leisure can develop leadership skills, for example through captaining a team or running a club.
notes.tip: Give physical, social and emotional development separate headed points, as questions usually name them. For physical, think fitness and skills; for social, teamwork and friends.

notes.h: Emotional and intellectual development through leisure
notes.b: Leisure also shapes how people feel and think. Examiners sometimes add intellectual development to physical, social and emotional development.
points: Emotional development: competitive activities can improve self-esteem and confidence, and give a sense of achievement.
Emotional development: relaxing pursuits such as yoga, reading or gardening reduce stress and support mental wellbeing.
Emotional development: being part of a team or community gives a sense of belonging, and coping with success and failure builds resilience.
Emotional development: fun and enjoyment encourage positive emotions and a positive outlook.
Intellectual development: card games, bridge, chess and puzzles develop concentration, analysis, problem solving and planning.
Intellectual development: debating and drama develop listening skills, argument and self-expression, and creative pursuits such as art encourage creativity and learning.
notes.tip: For emotional development, write about confidence, stress relief and belonging. Keep it separate from social development, which is about teamwork and friends.

notes.h: Social and cultural influences on leisure
notes.b: What people do in their free time is shaped by the society and culture around them, not only by personal taste.
points: Social group: a person's socio-economic group affects which activities are available and affordable.
Local factors: the clubs, facilities and transport in a person's area shape which activities they can join.
Trends: popular activities, such as skateboarding, spread through peer groups and the media, and greater access to foreign travel has made it a common leisure choice.
Technology, social media and education also shape leisure choices, because they change what people know about and can do.

Culture: traditions tied to a country or region, such as hurling, Gaelic football, camogie, Irish music and Irish dancing in Ireland. The GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association) is the national amateur sports body.
Religious and community traditions, and a family's ethnic and cultural background, also influence the activities people take up.
Family traditions: activities handed down through families, such as music or sport, shape a person's leisure from childhood, so children often take up the leisure activities their parents enjoy.
notes.tip: Questions on social and cultural influences want a short developed point per factor with an example. Use Irish examples such as hurling or Irish dancing for culture.

notes.h: Occupation and income as influences on leisure
notes.b: A person's job decides how much time and money they have for leisure, and even the kind of leisure they want.
points: Disposable income: the money left after essential spending determines how much can be spent on leisure.
Cost of leisure: membership fees, joining fees, pay-as-you-go charges and special clothing or equipment, plus travel, all add to the cost.
Low-cost choices: people with little disposable income often choose free or inexpensive activities, such as walking, the library or the park.
Working hours: long or irregular hours reduce the time available for leisure.
Type of work: a sedentary (desk-based) worker may choose an energetic activity, and an active worker may prefer a quiet pursuit, so leisure balances the job.
Leisure can be an extension of work, for example when a person's job involves sport or the arts, or when colleagues' clubs lead to a new pastime.
Part-time work, job-sharing and career breaks create more time for leisure.
Recession: a fall in income reduces spending on costly activities such as foreign holidays, while people spend more time on free or home-based activities.
notes.tip: For the effect of a recession on leisure, say that spending on costly leisure falls and people turn to free or low-cost choices. For cost, name the costs: fees, equipment, clothing and travel.

notes.b: Leisure changes as a family moves through the life cycle (the stages from young adults, to parents of young children, to retirement). The stage a person is at matters more than their age alone.
points: Young people have fewer commitments and more time for leisure, and teenagers often prefer to spend leisure time with their peers.
Couples with young children usually have the least time and disposable income for leisure, because childcare takes both.
Families with school-going children often have leisure built around school sport, clubs and outings.
Retired couples usually have more time and often more money for leisure.
Older people may have physical limits that restrict them to less strenuous or sedentary pursuits.
Some activities are regarded as too dangerous for young children, so families choose age-appropriate pursuits that are suitable and safe for them.
notes.tip: Link each leisure pattern to the life-cycle stage, for example young children bring the least time and money, and retirement brings the most. Give one developed point with an example per factor.

notes.b: Gender can affect which leisure activities people choose and how much time they have for them.
points: Some activities are male- or female-dominated, which can affect whether a person feels welcome to take part.
Gender affects the time available for leisure, because household and caring duties still fall mainly on women in many families. Traditionally women had less time for this reason.
Changing gender roles have reduced the strength of traditional divisions in leisure choices, and many sports and activities are now open to everyone, though some differences remain.
notes.tip: Questions pair gender with age, so give a clear point on each: time available and who dominates certain activities.

notes.b: Two further factors affect what a person can do in their leisure time.
points: Health and ability limit or shape the activities a person can take part in.
The facilities available locally decide which activities are within reach.

notes.h: Investigation: time-use record and costing leisure pursuits
notes.b: This practical shows how much of a day is really leisure and what leisure costs. It also lets you compare families at different stages of the life cycle.
points: Aim: to find out how a person spends their day and how much of that time is leisure.
Method step 1: keep a record of each hour of a typical day, noting each activity.
Method step 2: sort each entry into essential activities (sleep, personal care, paid work, household tasks) and leisure.
Method step 3: add the hours in each category and express the leisure time as a percentage of the day.
Method step 4: list each leisure pursuit and cost it, including membership fees, equipment, travel and pay-as-you-go charges.
Method step 5: list the physical, social, emotional and intellectual benefits of each pursuit beside its cost, so that value can be judged.
Case study method: compare the time-use records of families at different life-cycle stages, such as a young couple, a couple with young children, teenagers and a retired couple.

keyTerms.definition: The time left over after essential activities have been completed, which a person spends as they choose for relaxation or enjoyment.
Tasks that must be done, such as paid work, sleep, personal care, household tasks and caring for dependants.
The income left after essential spending, which can be used for leisure and other choices.
Leisure pursued alone or with people outside the family.
Leisure shared by members of one household, such as outings, games or sport together.
A classification of people by occupation and income, which influences their access to leisure activities.
Involving little physical movement, such as sitting for long periods.
Exercise in which the body's own weight is carried by the legs, such as walking or dancing, which helps keep bones strong.
The stage a family has reached, such as young children at home, school-going children or retirement, which shapes its leisure time and money.
A log of how each hour of a day is spent, used to measure the share of time given to leisure.

factCards.term: Four functions of leisure in today's society
factCards.definition: 1. Relaxation and relief from stress. 2. Physical wellbeing. 3. Skill development. 4. Social interaction and family bonding.

factCards.term: Three benefits of leisure for children's social development
factCards.definition: 1. Co-operation and communication in team sports. 2. Coping with winning and losing. 3. Making new friends and developing leadership skills.

factCards.term: Three factors that influence family leisure patterns
factCards.definition: 1. Occupation and income. 2. Age and life-cycle stage. 3. Culture and family traditions.

factCards.term: Two effects of a recession on family leisure
factCards.definition: 1. Less money is available for costly activities such as foreign holidays and school trips. 2. Families take up free activities such as walking, and spend more time together at home.

factCards.term: Two examples of weight-bearing leisure activities
factCards.definition: Walking and dancing, which carry the body's weight through the legs and help reduce the risk of osteoporosis.

questions.prompt: Define leisure and give two benefits of leisure for family members.
questions.model: Leisure: the time left over after essential activities such as paid work, sleep, personal care and household tasks have been completed, which a person spends as they choose for relaxation or enjoyment. Benefit 1: relaxation and relief from stress, which improves wellbeing. Benefit 2: family bonding and communication through shared activities, or social interaction that strengthens relationships. Two benefits are required for full marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how family leisure activities are influenced by age, occupation, culture and gender, and explain the role of leisure in the physical, social and emotional development of children.
questions.model: Age: young families have fewer commitments but couples with young children have least time and money; retired couples have more of both; older people may have physical limits that restrict them to sedentary pursuits. Occupation: disposable income and working hours decide the time and money available; sedentary workers may choose energetic activities; part-time work or job-sharing creates more time. Culture: regional and national traditions such as hurling, Irish music and Irish dancing shape family choices, and family traditions are passed on to children. Gender: some activities are dominated by one gender, and household and caring duties affect the time available. Physical development: sport builds fitness, muscle tone and coordination, and weight-bearing activities help reduce the risk of osteoporosis. Social development: team sports teach co-operation, communication, coping with success and failure, and making friends. Emotional development: competitive and relaxing pursuits build self-esteem, confidence, a sense of belonging and stress relief.
